observation: v1 shipped through full pipeline (architecture-critique 8/10, review DONE) despite a critical gap: the implementation was flag-only (emit session_not_returned event + record verdict), never force-blocking. AC1/AC3 demand 'not accepted as complete' + 'redirected to return' (forcing arms); v1 satisfied only the weak 'surfaced as not-yet-returned' (passive flag). The gates (architecture-critique, review) praised the elegant observer seam without challenging whether the weaker-arm implementation met the AC's strongest reading.

v1 never surveyed or rejected the SDK's native Stop hook or the Claude Agent SDK hook mechanism (both purpose-built for exactly this use case: blocking a turn-end and re-injecting guidance). Instead invented a passive observer-in-loop with no forcing capability. The re-architecture (v2) required switching to Hook + Stop (SDK adapter) and loop interception (builtin) for Tier-1 forcing. This violated ETHOS 'Search Before Building' — mechanism options were not explored before settling on an inferior design.

v1 shipped with only scripted tests (mock/stub LLM streams via cassettes) proving the observer and event emission worked. No live-LLM integration test / eval proved that a real agent on a real harness actually gets forced or accepts the non-returned verdict. This violated the project's own rule: 'agent-behavior ACs must have a live eval run via the LLM.' v1 passed /architecture-critique and /review without that proof.

v1's Re-injection observer was genuinely elegant in one dimension: +1 line per drain loop (at 760, 665), zero new adapter method, zero new event type, observes existing ToolCallEvent. The design optimized for simplicity but was _simple-weak_: the mechanism was insufficient. This exposes a process trap: the 'simplification lens' in architecture-critique can praise minimal implementation without verifying the minimal choice still satisfies the strongest AC reading.

v2 re-architecture required: (a) hook-based forcing (SDK Stop hook + builtin loop interception), (b) extended SessionOutcome union to include 'not_returned', (c) widened TriggerResult to carry returnVerdict + outcome as union, (d) per-adapter canForceReturn capability descriptor, (e) two-tier model (Tier-1 force, Tier-2 reject), and (f) live eval (force-return scenario run on real LLM). All could have been planned initially had the mechanism been surveyed and the live-eval requirement been gating v1's completion.

v2 live eval (force-return) scored 1.000/1.000 on deepseek-v4-pro (~$0.09 cost). The scenario had an agent deliberately tempted NOT to return; the forcing fired (>=1 re-injection), and the agent ultimately returned. This proved the mechanism works on real LLM behavior. v1 had no such proof.

v2 architecture-critique (round 1) scored 6/10 but identified a different critical: the v2 re-architecture had overlooked that bet-decomposition (extraction drain) was not wired. This was caught by the reviewer's re-grep and forced a concept refinement (internal-extraction-drain exemption). The critique process worked as designed on v2, but missed it on v1 (the v1 critique did not re-verify the two-sites claim against actual code).

Architecture-critique gates verify 'does the plan follow the spec?' but do not verify 'does the plan's design-chosen mechanism satisfy the strongest reading of the AC?'. On v1: the critique approved the observer-only design without asking whether observation + flag emission = 'not accepted as complete / redirected to return' in the AC's terms. Both lenses (support + adversarial) optimized within the chosen mechanism instead of challenging whether the mechanism met the bar. Candidate fix: a 'strongest-AC-reading audit' lens in critique when an AC has either/or language or force/passivity spectrum — explicitly ask 'does the architect's mechanism satisfy the strongest requirement, or the weakest?'

Review gates (code-review, architecture-critique) have no hook to require a live LLM eval for agent-behavior ACs. v1 passed code-review (reviewed the implementation structure) and critique (reviewed the plan) without anyone asking 'where is the proof that a real agent actually gets forced?' The DoD rule exists (agent-behavior ACs need live evals), but it is not integrated into the gate machinery. Candidate fix: /architecture skill should require a 'live eval coverage map' when the ACs quantify over agent behavior or system responses to agent actions — enumerate which evals will prove each AC, run them locally during build phase, and carry the proof into review. Defer an AC to 'live eval only' if a gate cannot verify it from code inspection alone.

Cost signal: v1 consumed ~3.5h (concept + architecture + build + review gates passing, then shipping to PR ready). v2 consumed ~4h additional (re-architecture phase, critique round 2, build green, review). Full cost impact: one complete pipeline cycle spent on an architecture that under-delivered, then a second cycle to correct it. The founder's rejection at the review gate would have been ideal; it happened after ship instead. Lesson: ship gate (/) missed a check — it should verify at `/ship` whether live-eval coverage exists for agent-behavior ACs before attestation.

v3-r1 (architecture critique round 1) scored 5/9 NEEDS-REVISION, catching a FABRICATED carrier. The plan claimed forcing would reach external (non-Claude) harnesses via `config.messages` + a prompt arg. The reviewer independently re-read the three external adapter implementations (cli, isolated, remote) and found: (1) cli-harness-adapter.ts:207-208 spawns with cwd:config.sandboxPath, uses only 5-var template {{sandbox}}{{model}}{{apiKey}}{{baseUrl}}{{mcpUrl}} (zero prompt arg, zero config.messages read); (2) isolated-harness-adapter.ts:128 forks SDK via child.send({type:'start', config}), inner SDK reads CLAUDE.md from cwd (not config.messages); (3) remote never reads config.messages (only builtin-harness-adapter.ts:389,474 does). The plan's §3.3 'adapters that read the prompt...also append the forcing message to the kickoff prompt the adapter passes' described an arg that DOES NOT EXIST. This is the SAME class of hole as v2 (forcing that doesn't reach external models), hidden deeper. The reviewer caught it by INDEPENDENT code-read, not trusting plan assertions.

v3-r1 critique was initially supposed to be a single APPROVED pass (like v1). Instead it scored 5/9 NEEDS-REVISION because the reviewer did NOT trust the plan's 'verified against code' assertions. This is a process discipline that SAVED v3 from shipping a hole: the reviewer explicitly re-grepped and re-read every adapter cited in the plan (context-assembly-prompt.ts, cli-harness-adapter.ts, isolated-harness-adapter.ts, claude-agent-sdk-adapter.ts). A less careful critic (one who took the plan's word) would have approved the false plan, it would have shipped, founder would have rejected it post-merge, and AL6 would need v4. The critique process WORKED because the reviewer treated 'verified against code' claims as hypothesis to verify, not fact to accept.

v3-r2 (critique round 2) approved 8/9 after the plan redesigned the forcing carrier from the fabricated `config.messages` to the REAL sandbox instruction-file rewrite. The fix: writeSandboxAgentsMd(sandboxPath, assembled_prompt + AL6_FORCE_RETURN_MESSAGE) before re-startSession. This carrier is real because: (1) writeSandboxAgentsMd exists at context-assembly-prompt.ts:277-279 and writes AGENTS.md+CLAUDE.md to the sandbox root; (2) every external adapter spawns with cwd:config.sandboxPath and re-reads that file on re-spawn; (3) grep confirms config.messages is read ONLY by builtin. The cost of the v3-r1 catch + redesign + v3-r2 re-critique: ~2.5h added to the timeline. If critique had not caught the fabrication, the false plan would have shipped and been founder-rejected again post-merge (the SAME error pattern as v1/v2 in a new disguise).

v3 live eval (scenario: fr-forced-return-external) tested forcing on a real external-shaped harness (hasNativeReturnHook:false, deepseek-v4-pro agent) via the Layer-B re-prompt loop. Result: 0.933/1.000 aggregate. Breakdown: force_return_injected = 1.0 (2 Layer-B re-engagements recorded, external agent was forced via sandbox-file rewrite), return_eventually_called_or_not_returned = 0.8 (agent remained stubborn even after forcing, correctly settled to not_returned not completed), not_silently_completed = 1.0 (no v1 regression). The score < 1.0 is honest: forcing DID reach the external agent (dimension 1), the agent chose not to comply (dimension 2 penalty). Contrast v2: v2's live eval (force-return) scored 1.0 on builtin (easy in-process path); the external path never ran in v2, so 1.0 gave false confidence. v3's 0.933 on the external path (the actually-required hardest path per 'uniform across harnesses') is the credible proof the founder demanded.

During v3 build (GREEN phase), the multi-spawn re-prompt loop was live during an Anthropic API 5xx outage. A spawn died server-side; the turn did not rollback. Instead it resumed from the next committed task boundary. This validates two things: (1) the re-prompt loop design (multiple startSession calls per turn) is durable to partial failures, and (2) the existing committed task boundary resume protocol is robust. No special checkpointing was needed; the existing turn-level granularity held. This is a positive signal for harnesses that spawn multiple times per turn (the cost of re-prompt loop is incurred upfront; the recovery is free if resume protocol is sound).

Independent review (Phase 4) happened after build and was performed by a different agent than the architect/builder. Review confirmed the plan against the BUILT code: (1) sandbox file is written with forcing message before re-startSession (not after); (2) loop bounds enforced (AL6_MAX_FORCE_RETURNS=2); (3) cost caps survive loop; (4) abort affordances survive loop. The fact that review was independent (different agent, different phase, different materials: built code not plan) is what enabled a second gate to catch slippage. v1/v2 had gates (architecture-critique, review) but both reviewed the same plan or same code without the two-stage separation. v3's critique→build→code-review separation with different reviewers is the structure that prevented another hole from shipping.

The v1/v2/v3 three-version arc + two post-merge rejections trace to a single root: NO GATE CHECKS WHETHER AC QUANTIFICATIONS (e.g., 'uniform across all harnesses') ARE MET FOR EVERY MEMBER OF THE QUANTIFIED SET, ONLY FOR THE HAPPY-PATH MEMBER. v1: AC4 says 'uniform forcing across CLI/sdk/isolated/builtin' → v1 only touches builtin → gates praised elegance, never asked 'for all harnesses?' → MISSED. v2: AC4 same → v2 touches SDK+builtin (hooks)+others (reject-only) → founder rejects 'not all can force' → MISSED. v3: AC4 same → v3 touches ALL (or claims to via fabricated carrier, caught by critique). The FIRST time 'all harnesses' requirement drove a gate decision is v3-r1 critique, and ONLY because a different failure (fabrication) made scope enumeration necessary. Candidate fix: when /architecture-critique encounters AC quantification language ('all X', 'regardless', 'uniform'), explicitly enumerate the set and ask 'does this mechanism satisfy the AC for EACH member, or degrade for some?'
